metadata.research_goal: Create backend-ready beginner, intermediate, and advanced boxing teaching progressions, assessments, promotion gates, and safe-contact rules.

key_concepts.summary: Beginners need stance, guard, movement, basic punches, simple defense, and low-threat partner awareness.
Intermediate boxers need variable combinations, defense-to-counter, range control, and constrained sparring.
Advanced boxers need style-specific tactics, fight-camp planning, sparring periodization, and tactical adjustment.
Contact progression requires defensive competency, coach control, readiness, and symptom monitoring.
Conditioning should not obscure whether a boxer actually understands the skill.
Promotion gates should include technical quality, decision-making, conditioning, and injury/readiness signals.

tactical_rules.rule: Beginner programs should not default to open sparring.
Progress punch variety only when stance and guard recovery remain stable.
Controlled sparring requires demonstrated block/parry/slip/exit basics.
Intermediate tactical learning should use constrained sparring with defined tasks.
Advanced work should connect tactics to opponent style, round score, and fight-camp phase.
Headache, dizziness, worsening hand pain, or poor recovery should hold or regress contact.

physical_demands.quality: basic strength, aerobic base, shoulder and trunk control
repeat punching bursts and footwork under controlled fatigue
style-specific power, pace control, and late-round quality
neck/trunk/shoulder preparation paired with defensive skill, not blind toughness
body composition and fueling managed slowly and safely

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Beginners may lack defense and awareness, increasing avoidable contact risk.
Intermediate athletes may escalate sparring before tactical control is ready.
Advanced camp can accumulate contact, weight, sleep, and stress load.
Painful hand/wrist impact should regress bag/pad volume and check wrapping/technique.
Any head symptom should block contact progression and trigger medical review.

training_implications.summary: Beginners can train boxing 2-4 days/week with low contact and simple conditioning.
Intermediate plans should split technical boxing, conditioning, and S&C while managing sparring.
Advanced fight-camp blocks should sequence base, specific sparring, peak, taper, and recovery.
Level changes require evidence, not just time elapsed.
Athlete state should store sparring rounds, contact intensity, symptoms, hand pain, and readiness.
